item.title: How to get into AI Overviews: Google uses half of its sources from outside the top results for Russian queries
item.description:
AI Overviews in Google are often seen as a Western phenomenon that doesn't concern Russian websites. I collected over a thousand Russian queries from fifty niches and checked Google's search results with the region set to Russia. AI Overviews appeared in 93% of cases, and half of their sources were not on the first page of regular search results. This means it's possible to get into an overview without being in the top results. Read more

item.title: We are like the world
item.description:
Everything we surround ourselves with is both a result of our thoughts and what we think with. Roads define geography, speed, distance, space. Trinkets on a dresser are memories, emotions. Tools on a desk are plans, skills. Our external environment doesn't tell us what to do, it guides us. Some things are softer, some harder, but we are not just the brain in a skull; we are also what was created before us and what we have created ourselves. This article is about what surrounds us and how it relates to LLMs and agents. Read more

item.title: Building a Raspberry Pi 5 Robot for My Daughter: More Than Just a Smart Speaker!
item.description:
I wanted a robot that could help my child and talk without the internet. This led me to test nearly twenty local AI models, select a voice, add a camera to a bow, and teach its eyes and head to track people. In the first part, I detail how a sketch became a working prototype and what went wrong along the way. Read on.

item.title: [Translation] Turning Off Your Brain Is Not a Good Sign
item.description:
Back in early 2025, I started noticing how people, when using AI, would put their brains into passive mode. They'd ask the AI to perform a task (summarize text, write code, etc.), accepting the result at face value. At the time, this approach worked very poorly, and the results were often nonsensical. But AI was developing, and I began to notice this behavior more and more often. Sometimes people would just ask the AI to write them code, which they would unconditionally accept as working. In other cases, a human was involved in the loop, monitoring the result and asking the AI to fix problems if they arose. Niklas Gruhn even coined a term for such people – meat proxy. Read more

item.title: Amazon will sell brands a piece of Alexa's response: promotion in neural networks will become partially paid
item.description:
On September 29, at the unBoxed conference, Amazon introduced the Branded Conversations format. The brand writes a brief about its products, and the Alexa for Shopping assistant relies on it when explaining to the buyer how one model differs from another. Until now, brands paid for a place next to the AI's answer. Now you can pay for a piece of the explanation itself. For those involved in promotion in neural networks, there are two questions: what to do with open models where there is no brief, and how to measure visibility when part of the answers are purchased. Read more

item.title: Chinese Children Who Stopped Doing Homework Themselves Faced Serious Difficulties in Exams
item.description:
A 30-month study of 27,000 Chinese schoolchildren found that those who started using generative AI did their homework faster and better, but stopped truly learning. Scores on closed-book tests (those without multiple-choice/essay questions) dropped by 20%, and on entrance exams by ~25%. We all strive to simplify tedious work using available tools. Initially, we invented writing instead of memorizing; abacuses and their younger sibling, the calculator, simplify our work with math, etc. Mnemonic rhymes like "Every hunter..." are similar tools, but existing in language. And much, much more... With enough desire, one can find a hundred more examples of how we expand our cognitive control zone using external tools. There's even a whole philosophical doctrine of externalism about this. I won't delve too deep, but I'll quote something necessary for my further analysis: Read more

item.title: Aquilum — a fast Obsidian alternative in Rust that consumes about 27MB of RAM
item.description:
Aquilum is a fast, local-first note-taking app written in Rust for Windows, consuming around 27MB of RAM with an 11MB installer. It features a knowledge graph, backlinks, live Markdown preview, multiple knowledge bases, advanced tables, books and a reader, Dataview-like data analysis, fast search, change history, and integration with MCP agents. A detailed review of its features and architecture is in the article. Learn more

item.title: How We Deploy AI to Production Sites, or What Happens After the "Fix It" Command
item.description:
In the first part, I talked about how we went from simply copying code between MODX and ChatGPT to a proper subject-oriented interface for the CMS. The agent stopped seeing the site as a jumble of files and database rows and gained the ability to work with resources, chunks, TVs, and their dependencies. At some point, this was enough to set tasks almost as I would set them for a developer, without detailed instructions on where exactly to go and which line to change. The next step was obvious. If the agent had already figured out the problem and found a solution, why should I take its code, connect via SSH, make a backup, upload the fix, run checks, and then browse the site to see if anything nearby broke? I wanted to simply write "See why the form stopped sending, fix it, and check" and get back not a ten-point instruction that I would have to execute myself, but an already fixed site. This is where the second part of our project began. Giving write access turned out to be quite simple. SSH, physical files, logs, a browser, and several utility tools were added to MODX MCP. Much more time was spent ensuring that after the "fix it" command, I wouldn't be hovering over the agent's shoulder, watching what exactly it was about to mess up. Read more

item.title: How to Create Banners with Neural Networks: AI for Advertising
item.description:
If you've ever been involved in advertising and marketing, you've likely encountered the need for a banner ad campaign. Doing it manually is time-consuming, and outsourcing costs money and time. Today, this can be done in under an hour, including approvals. The challenge isn't whether AI can draw, but whether it can capture attention, consider your audience, and meet platform requirements. While a large advertising campaign can hardly do without a designer, if you need prototypes or to quickly and cheaply generate several ad banners, you should know how to work with AI. Furthermore, the volume of creatives is growing faster than our ability to test them. So, what can be done? In this article, we'll explore which tools, and most importantly how, address banner advertising tasks, how to build a process where AI saves time, and where it only creates risks. Read on.

item.title: Astra codes space
item.description:
Lately, I've noticed that programmer acquaintances and strangers online are coding for fun. A friend recently sent me a link to a site with a 3D model of Earth and satellites, showing filters and orbits, using open-source data. He said he coded it in a couple of weeks. A few days later, he asked me to test a game he made, featuring orbital missions where you control a satellite and its orbit based on a physical model with formulas. Gameplay, achievements (like minimum impulse), and stars. It reminded me he always dreamed of coding games. And it made me think – I had similar dreams. Playing the first Mafia, I imagined coding a city simulation where every resident lived their own life. Playing old space strategy games like Master of Orion or X-COM, I dreamed of rewriting them with new graphics. But these dreams always ended with the realization of the immense effort required for design and programming after my day job. Now, 15-20 years later, I seem to have hit a midlife crisis. So what now? Now I'm Tony Stark, and my code is Jarvis. Read more

item.title: Local assistant for zooms, part 9: a week on Nemotron
item.description:
On Thursday, there was a 57-minute call with eight people. Nemotron labeled the participants' voices in 7 seconds. My microphone was still labeling with sherpa at the time. Then I ran the same track through the same code again and timed it: eighteen and a half minutes. I posted the eighth part in the evening of the release; there were no live meetings through the new engine yet. A week has passed. Read more
